meta: Michiel van Mierevelt's 1636 portrait of the diplomat François van Aerssen, aged 64, with his coat of arms.
about: Shown to the knees, François van Aerssen stands in a black coat with a large white ruff, one hand on a red-draped table, holding a striped glove. He was a diplomat in the service of the United Netherlands and lord of Sommelsdijk, De Plaat and Spijk. His quartered coat of arms is painted at the upper right, set in a chain with a medal. Michiel van Mierevelt dated the portrait 1636 at the upper left and wrote that the sitter was 64.

meta: Adriaen Coorte's 1685 still life of apricots, cherries, a chestnut and a butterfly on a stone ledge.
about: Apricots and cherries hang on a leafy branch against a dark ground. Below, on a pale stone ledge, lie a chestnut in its spiny husk and a red and white butterfly. Adriaen Coorte signed and dated the picture at lower right in 1685. In 1889 the Amsterdam dealers Van Pappelendam and Schouten sold it at Frederik Muller. It resurfaced at a Boston auction in 2006 under the label Dutch School, 17th Century Style, and the London dealer Richard Green bought it.

meta: Willem van Mieris's 1670 Allegory of Transience, a young woman pointing at a skull and a music book.
about: In a window, a young woman points to a skull and a music book lying on a Persian carpet on the sill. She holds flowers in her apron, a poppy grows in a pot at the right, and behind her a boy blows bubbles. The Rijksmuseum catalogues the picture as an allegory of transience, which fits the skull, the bubbles and the cut flowers. Willem van Mieris dated it 1670.

meta: Cima da Conegliano's Saint Jerome in the Wilderness, painted in the early 1500s and later owned by a Russian collector.
about: A bearded old man in a blue cloth kneels in the wilderness, looking upward and holding a stone. At the left a crucified figure hangs on a wooden cross, and a lion rests in the rocks. Beyond them a castle stands on a hill above a winding river. Cima da Conegliano painted it in the early 1500s. It was probably sold in London in the 1820s, and by the 1890s the Russian collector Alexander Orloff-Davidoff owned it in Saint Petersburg. Lord Lee of Fareham bought it in 1930, and the Kress Foundation gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1939.

meta: James Holland's 1850 view of the west side of Greenwich Hospital, painted for Richard Hollier.
about: Looking down what is now College Walk toward Grand Square, the picture shows the colonnaded west side of Greenwich Hospital with its dome and tall arched windows. Pensioners and other figures in period coats walk between the buildings. Richard Hollier of nearby Maze Hill commissioned James Holland to paint it in 1850. His widow gave it to the hospital in 1856. It was shown at the Royal Academy in 1851 and later in Paris. Holland painted a separate view from the east afterwards.

meta: Kano Tan'yu's ink painting of a spoonbill wading among water-grass.
about: Light touches of the brush stand for water and marsh grasses while a white spoonbill wades with its head bent low. A pale ink wash defines the bird against its white plumage. The museum finds in the painting the traits of Tan'yu's influential style, in which ink suggests form instead of describing it. He trained in Kyoto, moved to Edo in 1614, and became head of the Bureau of Painting, whose branch of the Kano school received major official commissions.

meta: Jan Antonisz van Ravesteyn's 1630 portrait of a man, once sold as a likeness of Hugo de Groot.
about: A man with a trimmed mustache and goatee looks out in a half-length portrait, wearing a dark doublet with shoulder lacing and a large pleated ruff. For a time he was taken for Hugo de Groot. Adriaan van der Hoop of Amsterdam bought the picture in the 1820s under that name, as a work by Abraham van den Tempel or Cornelis Janssens van Ceulen. He left it to the city in 1854 with the rest of his collection. It is now attributed to Jan Antonisz van Ravesteyn and hangs in the Rijksmuseum on loan.

meta: Pieter Bruegel the Elder's 1559 Netherlandish Proverbs, a village crowded with illustrated sayings.
about: Dozens of small figures act out Dutch proverbs in a crowded village. A man tumbles from a roof, people tip over a barrel, and others sit on a fence. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1559 on an oak panel. Wikipedia says its original title was The Blue Cloak or The Folly of the World, which suggests he meant a catalogue of human folly. Many faces have the blank look he gave his fools. His son Pieter Brueghel the Younger painted at least 16 copies, while the original is in Berlin.

meta: Thérèse Schwartze's 1883 portrait of Frederik Daniël Otto Obreen, head director of the Rijksmuseum, painted from a photograph.
about: Frederik Daniël Otto Obreen has white hair and a full white beard, and he wears a dark suit and waistcoat with a small red and white ribbon badge on his lapel. He was head director of the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam from 1883 to 1896. Thérèse Schwartze painted him from a photograph by Koene and Büttinghausen. She signed at lower left with the initials Th. v. D.S.

meta: Dominic Serres's The Piazza at Havana, British troops in the Plaza Vieja after the city's capture.
about: Redcoats parade in the Plaza Vieja of Havana, with sailors in the foreground and a stone fountain at the lower right. The picture shows the city under British occupation, after Britain took it from Spain in the Seven Years' War. Dominic Serres, a French-born British artist, painted a series on the taking of Havana for the Keppel family, three of whom led the campaign. This one had a pair, The Cathedral at Havana. The title uses piazza, an Italian loan word common in English at the time.

meta: The Penitent Magdalene, a lost Dresden painting traditionally given to Correggio.
about: Magdalen lies half raised under leafy rocks, her head on one arm and her eyes on an open book. Her ointment jar stands beside her head, her feet are bare, and a blue mantle flows around her body. Wikipedia calls the date of the painting uncertain and says the attribution to Correggio is traditional but disputed. It was last in the Dresden gallery and went missing after the Second World War.

meta: Ford Madox Brown's 1842 Manfred on the Jungfrau, taken from Byron's dramatic poem.
about: Manfred, a wealthy aristocrat from Byron's poem, stands on the Jungfrau about to throw himself from the heights. A chamois hunter in fur comes up in the background and will save him. Ford Madox Brown painted it in 1842, drawing on a speech in Act I Scene II where Manfred sees tall pines dwindle to shrubs far below. Wikipedia reads his face as showing deep psychological agony. John Martin had painted a watercolour of the same subject in 1837 that centred on the mountain.

meta: Jacopo de' Barbari's 1508 portrait of Albrecht of Brandenburg at eighteen, dressed for a church career.
about: Albrecht of Brandenburg is shown at eighteen as a candidate for church office, in a white surplice and a red biretta. His upward gaze signals the calling ahead of him. The gold brocade cope has a large silver clasp set with saints, which the catalogue text reads as a sign of his taste for display and his ambition even then. A signet ring sits on his right thumb. Jacopo de' Barbari painted him in 1508. The picture later belonged to the dukes of Anhalt at Wörlitz and Dessau.

meta: Jan Willem Pieneman's allegory on the death of William V, Prince of Orange, in 1806.
about: The Dutch Maid stands grieving at the prince's grave while an angel comforts her. A white marble bust of the prince sits on the grave, and two putti carry the coat of arms above it. At lower right the Dutch Lion sleeps on broken weapons. Jan Willem Pieneman signed the work on the gravestone. William V died in 1806, and the painting carries that year in its title.

meta: Ike Taiga's hanging scroll of a river valley and fishing town in spring.
about: Ike Taiga began by selling paintings on fans to earn a living after his father died young. He went on to find a place in Kyoto's literati community and became one of its leading figures, says the museum. In this colorful scroll a river flows down from a mountain village and passes through farms on its way to a fishing town among trees and bamboo. Two people set out in a boat on the calm water where the river widens.

meta: Pieter Saenredam's 1641 view of the nave and choir of St Mary's Church in Utrecht.
about: Visitors walk near the choir screen and by the pillar painted with a bull, in the nave of St Mary's Church in Utrecht, seen from the west. Two dogs play at the left. Pieter Saenredam wrote at lower right that he finished the picture on 29 January 1641 and signed it as made by him. The long view down the nave runs between tall pillars under arched vaults.

meta: Charles Hasslewood Shannon's 1907 portrait of Kathleen Bruce, later Lady Scott, in a hoop skirt.
about: Miss Kathleen Bruce, later Lady Scott and widow of the Antarctic explorer Sir Robert F. Scott, sits before a shadowed screen. The museum says her identity counts for less than her treatment as a decorous object, as the original title Souvenir of an International Ball suggests. Shannon posed her so that her hoop skirt billows out and fills the large chair. The museum sees a bouquet of fabrics and bows bursting from the real bouquet in her lap, and links the loose brushwork to Titian.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: François-Thomas Mondon's 1730 chinoiserie print of Amida, a Japanese god of navigation.
about: A deity sits on top of rocaille ornament with the sea behind him, and at the left a kneeling man holds his arms up to the sky. Below, a man's legs stick out of a cave-like hole in the ornament, and the title promises the manner in which one drowns in the god's honor. Cartouches, a crescent moon, shells and scrolling leaves fill the design. François-Thomas Mondon made the plate in 1730, and the museum calls it chinoiserie, a European style inspired by fanciful ideas of China and East Asia.

meta: Artemisia Gentileschi's 1612 Danaë, a reclining nude generally taken as the artist's self-portrait.
about: A reclining woman lies on white linen and a red velvet cover, her eyes closed and one arm raised behind her head. A servant in a blue skirt and white headscarf holds a cloth above her while small golden specks fall through the air. Artemisia Gentileschi painted it in 1612. Wikipedia says it is assumed to be a self-portrait of the artist. The painting hangs in the Saint Louis Art Museum.
